outline.chapter_title: The Dispute’s Setting: Refugee Admissions, Funding, and the Statutory Framework
outline.description: This chapter introduces the legal regime and factual events that produced the litigation. It explains the two executive orders, the structure of the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program, the plaintiffs’ identities and interests, and the statutory provisions that matter most to the panel’s order: the President’s entry-suspension authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f), the Refugee Act framework, the APA challenge to agency action, and the domestic resettlement provisions in 8 U.S.C. § 1522.
subtopics: The January 20, 2025 executive order 'Realigning the United States Refugee Admissions Program' and its suspension of refugee entry
The President’s asserted authority under 8 U.S.C. §§ 1182(f) and 1185(a)
The January 24, 2025 suspension of USRAP funding under the separate foreign-aid executive order
How refugee admissions and post-admission resettlement services are distinct components of USRAP
The plaintiffs: approved refugees abroad, refugees already admitted to the United States, and nonprofit resettlement/processing organizations
The causes of action: Refugee Act challenge to the admissions suspension and APA challenges to the funding suspension and related agency actions
Why Negusie v. Holder is cited: the Refugee Act as a general framework for the treatment of refugees
The domestic resettlement provisions in 8 U.S.C. § 1522, including reception and placement, cash and medical assistance, and services for unaccompanied minors
The role of cooperative agreements with nonprofit agencies in delivering refugee services
Congressional appropriations and reporting requirements referenced by the panel as context for the statutory duty question

outline.chapter_title: From District Court Injunctions to an Interim Appellate Stay
outline.description: This chapter traces the case’s procedural posture, which is essential to understanding the order. It explains what the district court enjoined, how the government responded, what the Ninth Circuit had already done through earlier partial stays and carveouts, and why the current order is an interim stay pending a later merits opinion rather than the final appellate resolution.
subtopics: The February 2025 filing in the Western District of Washington

The February 28 written order clarifying that the injunction also barred suspension of USRAP funding
The government’s February 26 termination of cooperative agreements for domestic reception and placement and overseas processing support
The district court’s March 24 preliminary injunction ordering reinstatement of the terminated cooperative agreements
The government’s notices of appeal from the February 28 and March 24 orders
The Ninth Circuit motions panel’s March 25 partial stay and its reliance on Trump v. Hawaii
The carveout for individuals conditionally approved for refugee status before January 20, 2025, and the later April 21 and May 9 clarification orders
The district court’s July 14 enforcement framework and magistrate-judge supervision of the carveout
The government’s July 17 emergency motion, the Ninth Circuit’s July 18 administrative stay, expedited argument, and submission for decision
Why the panel vacates prior administrative and partial stays and replaces them with a new stay order pending appeal

outline.chapter_title: The Stay Standard and the Panel’s Treatment of the Refugee-Admissions Suspension
outline.description: This chapter explains the governing stay-pending-appeal framework and shows how the panel applies it to the challenge against the President’s suspension of refugee entry. The emphasis is on the relationship between Nken v. Holder and Trump v. Hawaii, and on why the panel concludes that the government is likely to succeed on this part of the case.

Why the district court’s injunctions are stayed insofar as they block the refugee-admissions suspension
The significance of the panel issuing only an interim order now and reserving fuller merits analysis for a later opinion

outline.chapter_title: The APA and Resettlement-Services Issue: Why the Panel Preserves Limited Relief
outline.description: This chapter isolates the part of the case on which the government does not, in the panel’s view, have a strong likelihood of success. It examines the panel’s reading of 8 U.S.C. § 1522, the evidence about the government’s termination of cooperative agreements, and the narrow affirmative directive requiring reinstatement of agreements necessary to provide post-admission reception and placement services.

How this limited exception reshapes the stay: the injunctions are otherwise stayed in full, but relief survives for admitted refugees’ post-arrival services

outline.chapter_title: Judge Lee’s Partial Dissent and the Opinion’s Broader Significance
outline.description: This chapter analyzes Judge Lee’s concurrence in part and dissent in part, which frames the central interpretive disagreement over § 1522. It also explains what this interim order does and does not decide, and why the case matters as a study in presidential immigration power, statutory limits on agency defunding, and appellate management of emergency relief.
